paper.title_en: Extremal micro black holes and antimatter: A cautious mathematical analogy at the Planck boundary of gravity and quantum theory
paper.abstract_en: Antimatter is normally defined in quantum field theory by charge conjugation of particle states, whereas black holes are classical or semiclassical spacetime solutions characterized externally by mass, angular momentum, and gauge charges. For this reason, an extremal micro black hole should not be identified with antimatter in the usual particle-physics sense. Nevertheless, charged extremal black holes provide a precise mathematical arena in which several structures familiar from matter–antimatter physics reappear: charge conjugation, pair creation, annihilation-like neutralization, and particle–antiparticle production in strong fields. Motivated by the proposal of Haug and Spavieri that extremal Reissner–Nordström micro black holes could set ultimate limits on battery energy density, and by the broader relevance of ultra-high-density energy to far-future space propulsion, we examine these formal similarities while explicitly avoiding a conclusive identification. We emphasize that Planck-scale extremal Reissner–Nordström objects lie at, or beyond, the domain where classical general relativity can be trusted without quantum corrections. Since there is no consensus theory unifying gravity and quantum mechanics, such objects should be treated as theoretical probes of the interface between the two frameworks. The key observation is that the Reissner–Nordström metric is invariant under <math altimg="si1.svg" display="inline" id="d1e289"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>→</mo><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>, while the electromagnetic potential changes sign. Thus a positively charged extremal micro black hole and a negatively charged extremal micro black hole are geometrically identical but electromagnetically conjugate. Their extremal charge-to-mass relation plays a role analogous to the charge-to-mass ratio of elementary particles and antiparticles, while Hawking radiation and Schwinger discharge provide quantum channels in which black-hole physics meets particle–antiparticle production. We suggest that the analogy may be useful as a heuristic guide to possible quantum-gravity questions, but only as an invitation to further work: many conceptual, mathematical, and experimental steps remain before any such connection could be regarded as physically established. To make the scope quantitative, we also test four consistency conditions that are essential at the Planck boundary: electric-charge quantization, the black-hole area bound on merger energy, Schwinger discharge, and the non-smoothness of the extremal limit once quantum corrections are included. These checks substantially restrict any literal storage interpretation. •Extremal R-N micro black holes mimic antimatter: <math altimg="si1.svg" display="inline" id="d1e315"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>→</mo><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> keeps geometry, flips potential.•Extremal micro black holes link charge–mass limits to annihilation and energy storage.•Hawking radiation and Schwinger discharge link charged holes to pair production.
